content:
Quick answer: There is no single best sleep position for joint pain. Most people do well lying on their side with a pillow between the knees, or on their back with a pillow under the knees. Keep the painful joint supported and in a comfortable middle position, and change position if it starts to ache. If pain wakes you most nights, see your GP or physiotherapist.

Good research on the "best" sleep position is limited, and what suits one person's knees may not suit another's shoulder. The practical aim is simple: support sore joints so they rest in a comfortable, middle position, and avoid positions that twist or squash them for hours. For a fuller plan on night pain, waking at 3am and when to get help, read our main how to sleep with arthritis guide.

Positions by painful joint

Knees

  • On your side, put a pillow between your knees so they do not press together
  • On your back, a pillow under the knees can ease strain, but some people find the knee stiffens if it stays bent all night. Try a thinner pillow if so

Hips

  • Lie on the less painful side with a pillow between your knees, which keeps the top hip level
  • If lying on either side hurts, try your back with a pillow under the knees
  • A softer mattress topper can ease pressure on the hip you lie on

Lower back

  • On your side, draw your knees up slightly with a pillow between them
  • On your back, put a pillow under your knees
  • Lying on your front often arches the back and twists the neck, so many people find it worse

Shoulders

  • Lie on the side that is not painful and hug a pillow so the sore arm rests on it
  • On your back, a small pillow under the painful arm can stop it dropping back
  • Avoid sleeping with your arm above your head

Neck and hands

  • Use enough pillow to keep your neck in line with your spine, not propped up or dropped down
  • For painful hands or wrists, rest them on a pillow; ask a physiotherapist or occupational therapist whether a night splint could help

Small changes that make positions work

  • Do gentle movement or a warm shower before bed so joints are less stiff
  • Time pain relief as your GP or pharmacist advises; our pain relief guide explains the options
  • Keep a spare pillow in bed so you can reposition without getting up
  • Turning over during the night is normal. If it hurts, bend your knees and roll as one unit

When to see your GP

  • Pain wakes you most nights, or night pain is new or getting worse
  • A joint is hot, red and swollen, or you feel unwell with fever
  • You snore loudly and feel very sleepy in the day, which can be a sign of sleep apnoea
  • Poor sleep has lasted months. The NHS recommends talking therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) before sleeping tablets, which can raise the risk of falls; see our sleeping tablets and falls guide

Frequently asked questions

Is sleeping on your back best for arthritis?

Not for everyone. Back sleeping with a pillow under the knees suits many people with back or knee pain, while side sleeping with a pillow between the knees often suits hips.

Do I need a special mattress?

There is no one best mattress for arthritis. A medium-firm mattress or a topper that eases pressure points suits many people. Try before you buy where you can.

Daytime activity helps nights too. See the exercise hub, our pacing guide and the flare-up guide for bad nights during a flare.
